In [[abstract algebra]], specifically the theory of [[Lie algebra]]s, '''Serre's theorem''' states: given a (finite reduced) [[root system]] <math>\Phi</math>, there exists a finite-dimensional [[semisimple Lie algebra]] whose root system is the given <math>\Phi</math>. It is named after [[Jean-Pierre Serre]].

== Statement ==
Given a root system <math>\Phi</math> in a [[Euclidean space]] with an inner product <math>(\cdot,\cdot)</math>, and the usual [[bilinear form]]  <math>\langle \beta, \alpha \rangle = 2(\alpha, \beta)/(\alpha, \alpha)</math>, with a fixed base <math>\{ \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \}</math>, there exists a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> generated by the <math>3n</math> elements <math>e_i, f_i, h_i</math> (for <math>1\leq i\leq n</math>) and relations:
:<math>[h_i, h_j] = 0,</math>
:<math>[e_i, f_j] = \delta_{ij}h_i,</math>
:<math>[h_i, e_j] = \langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle e_j, \, [h_i, f_j] = -\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle f_j,</math>
:<math>\operatorname{ad}(e_i)^{-\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle+1}(e_j) = 0, i \ne j, </math>
:<math>\operatorname{ad}(f_i)^{-\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle+1}(f_j) = 0, i \ne j. </math>
We also have that <math>\mathfrak g</math> is a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra with the Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak h = \bigoplus_{i}h_i</math> and that the root system of <math>\mathfrak g</math> is <math>\Phi</math>.

The [[square matrix]] <math>[\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle]_{1 \le i, j \le n}</math> is called the [[Cartan matrix]]. Thus, with this notion, the theorem states that, given a Cartan matrix ''A'', there exists a unique (up to an isomorphism) finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g(A)</math> associated to <math>A</math>. The construction of a semisimple Lie algebra from a Cartan matrix can be generalized by weakening the definition of a Cartan matrix. The (generally infinite-dimensional) Lie algebra associated to a [[generalized Cartan matrix]] is called a [[Kac–Moody algebra]].

== Sketch of proof ==
The proof here is taken from {{harv|Serre|1966|loc=Ch. VI, Appendix.}} and {{harv|Kac|1990|loc=Theorem 1.2.}}.<ref>{{cite book |last=Serre |first=Jean-Pierre |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7AHsSUrooSsC&pg=PA3 |title=Algèbres de Lie semi-simples complexes |date=1966 |publisher=Benjamin |isbn=978-3-540-67827-4 |language=en |translator-last=Jones |translator-first=G. A. |trans-title=Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras |authorlink=Jean-Pierre Serre}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Kac |first=Victor |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kuEjSb9teJwC&dq=Victor%20G.%20Kac&pg=PP1 |title=Infinite dimensional Lie algebras |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=1990 |isbn=0-521-46693-8 |edition=3rd |authorlink=Victor Kac}}</ref> Let <math>a_{ij} = \langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle</math> and then let <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g}</math> be the Lie algebra generated by (1) the generators <math>e_i, f_i, h_i</math> and (2) the relations:
*<math>[h_i, h_j] = 0,</math>
*<math>[e_i, f_i] = h_i</math>, <math>[e_i, f_j] = 0, i \ne j,</math>
*<math>[h_i, e_j] = a_{ij} e_j, [h_i, f_j] = -a_{ij} f_j.</math>

Let <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> be the free [[vector space]] spanned by <math>h_i</math>, ''V'' the free vector space with a basis <math>v_1, \dots, v_n</math> and <math display="inline">T = \bigoplus_{l=0}^{\infty} V^{\otimes l}</math> the [[tensor algebra]] over it. Consider the following representation of a Lie algebra:
:<math>\pi : \widetilde{\mathfrak g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(T)</math>
given by: for <math>a \in T, h \in \mathfrak{h}, \lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math>,
*<math>\pi(f_i)a = v_i \otimes a,</math>
*<math>\pi(h)1 = \langle \lambda, \, h \rangle 1, \pi(h)(v_j \otimes a) = -\langle \alpha_j, h \rangle v_j \otimes a + v_j \otimes \pi(h)a,</math> inductively,
*<math>\pi(e_i)1 = 0, \, \pi(e_i)(v_j \otimes a) = \delta_{ij} h_i(a) + v_j \otimes \pi(e_i)a,</math> inductively.
It is not trivial that this is indeed a well-defined representation and that has to be checked by hand. From this representation, one deduces the following properties: let <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_+</math> (resp. <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_-</math>) the subalgebras of <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g}</math> generated by the <math>e_i</math>'s (resp. the <math>f_i</math>'s).
*<math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_+</math> (resp. <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_-</math>) is a [[free Lie algebra]] generated by the <math>e_i</math>'s (resp. the <math>f_i</math>'s).
*As a vector space, <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g} = \widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_+ \bigoplus \mathfrak{h} \bigoplus \widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_-</math>.
*<math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_+ = \bigoplus_{0 \ne \alpha \in Q_+} \widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{\alpha}</math> where <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{\alpha} = \{ x \in \widetilde{\mathfrak g}|[h, x] = \alpha(h) x, h \in \mathfrak h \}</math> and, similarly, <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak{n}}_- = \bigoplus_{0 \ne \alpha \in Q_+} \widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{-\alpha}</math>.
*(root space decomposition) <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g} = \left( \bigoplus_{0 \ne \alpha \in Q_+} \widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{-\alpha} \right) \bigoplus \mathfrak h \bigoplus \left( \bigoplus_{0 \ne \alpha \in Q_+} \widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{\alpha} \right)</math>.

For each ideal <math>\mathfrak i</math> of <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g}</math>, one can easily show that <math>\mathfrak i</math> is homogeneous with respect to the grading given by the root space decomposition; i.e., <math>\mathfrak i = \bigoplus_{\alpha} (\widetilde{\mathfrak g}_{\alpha} \cap \mathfrak i)</math>. It follows that the sum of ideals intersecting <math>\mathfrak h</math> trivially, it itself intersects <math>\mathfrak h</math> trivially. Let <math>\mathfrak r</math> be the sum of all ideals intersecting <math>\mathfrak h</math> trivially. Then there is a vector space decomposition: <math>\mathfrak r = (\mathfrak r \cap \widetilde{\mathfrak n}_-) \oplus (\mathfrak r \cap \widetilde{\mathfrak n}_+)</math>. In fact, it is a <math>\widetilde{\mathfrak g}</math>-module decomposition. Let
:<math>\mathfrak g = \widetilde{\mathfrak g}/\mathfrak r.</math>
Then it contains a copy of <math>\mathfrak h</math>, which is identified with <math>\mathfrak h</math> and
:<math>\mathfrak g = \mathfrak{n}_+ \bigoplus \mathfrak{h} \bigoplus \mathfrak{n}_-</math> 
where <math>\mathfrak{n}_+</math> (resp. <math>\mathfrak{n}_-</math>) are the subalgebras generated by the images of <math>e_i</math>'s (resp. the images of <math>f_i</math>'s).

One then shows: (1) the derived algebra <math>[\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]</math> here is the same as <math>\mathfrak g</math> in the lead, (2) it is finite-dimensional and semisimple and (3) <math>[\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g] = \mathfrak g</math>.<!-- this needs to be explained better. -->
